new_entities.name: Long-term low-FODMAP diet
new_entities.description: Ongoing restriction of fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols over weeks to months.

new_entities.name: Gut microbiome diversity
new_entities.description: Diversity of the intestinal microbial community, including alpha-diversity indices and overall community richness.

edges.effect_quant: The best crossover diet trial found a low-FODMAP phase produced greater microbial diversity while simultaneously reducing total bacterial abundance, which is exactly why the long-term microbiome story stays mixed. Later clinical and review literature keeps that ambivalence: symptoms often improve, but the microbiome consequences are not uniformly reassuring.
edges.population: adults with irritable bowel syndrome or related gut symptoms following low-FODMAP dietary restriction for weeks to months
edges.mechanism: Reducing fermentable substrates can relieve osmotic and gas-driven IBS symptoms, but it can also reduce fermentable input for commensal organisms, so symptom benefit and microbial richness do not necessarily move in the same direction.
edges.summary: A long-term low-FODMAP diet should be treated as microbiome-mixed rather than simply beneficial or harmful. The diet can change the colonic environment in ways that improve symptoms, but sustained restriction may also suppress total bacterial abundance or specific beneficial taxa even when headline diversity metrics do not worsen.
edges.caveats: This edge is about microbial diversity, not symptom relief. It also does not imply the diet is unsafe; it means prolonged restriction should ideally be structured and liberalized when possible rather than followed indefinitely without reassessment.

evidence.notes: Diets that differ in their FODMAP content alter the colonic luminal microenvironment.
